title: A Sharp Effective Constant for the Diagonal Beta Correction Rate

problemStatement.formal: Let $q(n) = B(n+1,n+1)/T(n)$ with $T(n) = \sqrt{\pi n}/((2n+1)\,4^n)$. The parent proof gives $|q(n)-1| \le 3/n$. Improve the constant: prove $|q(n)-1| \le C/n$ for an explicit $C < 3$ (ideally $C \to 1/8$ for large $n$), and identify the sharp first-order coefficient $c_1 = \lim_{n\to\infty} n\,(q(n)-1) = \tfrac{1}{8}$, so that $q(n) - 1 = \tfrac{1}{8n} + O(1/n^2)$.
problemStatement.plain: The parent entry certifies that the diagonal Beta value matches its leading term with relative error at most 3/n, where the constant 3 is a convenient over-estimate from cheap exponential inequalities. The true leading error is q(n) - 1 ≈ 1/(8n), about 24 times smaller. This problem asks to prove an honest effective constant approaching the sharp value 1/8 and to pin down 1/8 as the exact first-order coefficient.
whyMatters: Turns the parent's order-correct bound into a magnitude-correct numerical error bar, usable for bounding symmetric Beta(n+1,n+1) normalising constants and the mass of the density t^n(1-t)^n.
Validates the parent's own stated open question and shows the telescoping Stirling-tail machinery can be pushed from an O(1/n) envelope to a sharp leading coefficient.
